claim: Random sampling (draw one architecture, zero search cost, expected performance equals the average of the search space) and random search (draw+evaluate many samples, keep the best-so-far incumbent, run for the same time budget as competing methods) are formally distinct baselines, and NAS papers must compare against both to separate search-space quality from search-algorithm quality.
stance_target: the precise definitional standard a NAS paper claiming to beat 'random search' must meet -- directly relevant to whether a target paper conflates random sampling with random search
scope_conditions: formal definitions (Definition 9, 10) proposed as community best practice
quoted_support: Random sampling draws a single random sample from the architecture space and returns it... Random search draws random samples from the architecture space, evaluates them..., and keeps track of the incumbent architecture with the best evaluation so far.

claim: NAS methods are almost always stochastic, so best practice requires reporting mean and standard deviation (or median/quartiles) across multiple runs with different seeds, and releasing the exact seeds used, rather than reporting a single run's result.
stance_target: the seed/repetition standard a paper claiming an LLM 'beats random search' must satisfy to be credible
quoted_support: we recommend that, if possible in terms of compute budgets, all methods should be repeated several times with different seeds and the authors should report mean and standard deviation... Ideally, one would control and report all used random seeds in a reproducible and simple sequence.

claim: A formal NAS benchmark requires a fixed dataset, fixed search space, and runnable code with pre-defined hyperparameters; tabular benchmarks (NAS-Bench-101 with 423k architectures, NAS-Bench-201 with 6k, NAS-Bench-1Shot1, NAS-Bench-NLP) and surrogate benchmarks (NAS-Bench-301, up to 10^18 architectures) are the recommended gold standard because they eliminate training-pipeline confounds via lookup instead of retraining.
stance_target: which benchmarks are considered methodologically rigorous by NAS reviewers, directly relevant to whether a target paper's search space (e.g. a custom CNN space) meets the bar or needs justification for not using a tabular benchmark
scope_conditions: definitions and Table 1 overview of available benchmarks as of 2019-2020
quoted_support: Tabular NAS benchmarks speed up experimentation dramatically compared to NAS benchmarks that involve training neural networks for every evaluation, as they replace this expensive step by a table lookup.

claim: Two distinct NAS evaluation variants exist and must not be conflated: the 'architecture identification variant' counts only the compute to identify the final architecture, while the 'AutoML variant' also counts the compute to train that architecture to a usable model -- a paper must specify which estimand its compute-budget comparison uses.
stance_target: the correct estimand distinction a NAS paper's compute-matched comparison against random search must specify, directly bearing on the query's mean-of-population vs expected-best-of-k question
quoted_support: In this variant, only the compute resources for identifying and returning the final architecture counts... In this variant, next to the compute resources for identifying the final architecture, we also count the compute resources to train the final architecture and return a model.

claim: Training-protocol engineering (Cutout, ScheduledDropPath, auxiliary towers, AutoAugment, more channels, more epochs) contributed a combined 3% test-accuracy improvement on CIFAR-10 in the DARTS search space, compared to less than 1% improvement from choosing the best architecture -- meaning final performance numbers from different NAS papers are incomparable unless the training pipeline is identical and released.
stance_target: the requirement that a NAS paper release its full training pipeline for any performance claim (including an LLM-guided one) to be comparable to prior work
scope_conditions: citing Yang et al. 2020's DARTS/CIFAR-10 ablation
quoted_support: the combination of CutOut, ScheduledDropPath, auxiliary towers, Auto-Augment, increasing the number of channels and increasing the number of epochs for training yielded a combined improvement of 3% test accuracy, compared to less than 1% for choosing the best neural architecture.

claim: The paper recommends running ablation studies to isolate which NAS-pipeline component (search space, training protocol, or search algorithm itself) is responsible for reported performance gains, since most published gains conflate these factors.
stance_target: the ablation standard a NAS paper (including LLM-guided NAS) must meet to credibly attribute performance gains to the search algorithm
scope_conditions: proposed best practice, citing prior confounding evidence from Sciuto et al., Li & Talwalkar, Yang et al.
quoted_support: we recommend to run ablation analyses to study the importance of individual components that affect performance, incl. any changes of the NAS benchmark and the NAS method itself.

claim: By 2019-2020, ICML and NeurIPS had begun requiring authors to complete Joelle Pineau's reproducibility checklist as part of paper submission, with reduced acceptance probability for papers that fail to justify withholding code -- establishing reproducibility disclosure as a normative reviewing bar in top ML venues.
stance_target: the reviewing-norms bar (code/seed/hyperparameter disclosure) a 2025-2026 NAS submission would be expected to clear
scope_conditions: ICML and NeurIPS submission process circa 2019-2020
quoted_support: the trend at top machine learning venues is going towards authors having to justify cases in which code is not made available (and where the acceptance probability is reduced when no good reasons exist).
